text:
Saraffian c. Syndicat de la
copropriété Villa Veritas phase 1

2017 QCCS 2230

JW0135

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-016942-032

500-17-020961-044

500-17-020464-049

DATE:

Le 12 mai 2017

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

ANDRÉ WERY, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

No: 500-17-016942-032

HANNA SARAFFIAN

Plaintiff

vs.

SYNDICAT DE LA COPROPRIÉTÉ
VILLA VERITAS PHASE 1 – and -

ILAN REIGH – and -

DARIO PIETRANTONIO

Defendants

No:
500-17-020961-044

ILAN REICH

Plaintiff

Vs.

HANNA SARAFFIAN

Defendant

No:
500-17-020464-049

DARIO PIETRANTONIO

Plaintiff

Vs.

HANNA SARAFFIAN

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[T]he Court is of the opinion that [Mrs.
Saraffian] is part of the problem, if not the problem itself.
[1]

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

This case is a sad illustration of what
constitutes bad faith, harassment and abusive conduct in a protracted dispute
and litigation by an owner of a unit in a condominium building.

CONTEXT

[
2
]

In August of 2000, Plaintiff Hanna Saraffian
buys on plans for 393 813$ apartment unit #306 at a 27 units condominium
complex known as
Villa Veritas Phase 1,

in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, in Montreal. She was eventually among the first
co-owners to take possession of her unit.

[
3
]

At about the same time, defendants Reich and
Pietrantonio each purchase a unit at the same location.

[
4
]

In the autumn of 2002, the defendants take
possession of their unit. Plaintiff Saraffian has already taken possession of
hers.

[
5
]

The work at the site is not completely finished.

[
6
]

In November, the promoter calls a meeting of the
new co-owners in order to proceed to the transition of the administration of
the Syndicate. Up to that date, the promoter had administered the affairs of
the Syndicate.

[
7
]

Defendants Reich and Pietrantonio are elected as
administrators with a third co-owner Claude Lambert. The co-owners had thus
elected respectively an engineer, a lawyer and a chartered accountant.

[
8
]

When they take over the affairs of the
Syndicate, things are not good. Many condo fees have not been collected (among
which those of plaintiff Saraffian), bills have not been paid and contractors
have not been hired for the maintenance of the property. There is an urgency to
react especially with winter being just around the corner.

[
9
]

The administrators work hard. They hold numerous
meetings during the evenings and the weekends in order to do everything that
has to be done.

[
10
]

The three of them have full-time professional
careers but they do that in order to protect their homes and that of the other
co-owners.

[
11
]

In the meantime, plaintiff Saraffian who had had
a grudge against the builder/promoter from the very start turns her attention
to the newly elected administrators of the Syndicate.

[
12
]

Things started to get nasty as soon as the
administrators attempted to collect the unpaid condo fees. Plaintiff Saraffian
resisted any payment considering that whatever resentment she had about the
builder/promoter justified her not to pay those condo fees.

[
13
]

The Syndicate was able to collect all the
arrears from every other co-owner except for plaintiff Saraffian. With the hard
work of the administrators, the affairs of the condominium got eventually back
on track.

[
14
]

Yet, plaintiff Saraffian was not happy.

[
15
]

She complained about a lot of things. She started
sending long single-lined letters to the administrators. She was also sending
urgent faxes and making regular phone calls to the administrators.

[
16
]

Whatever the administrators did or did not
wasn’t satisfactory to plaintiff.

[
17
]

This brought more and longer letters and more
phone calls where insults and threats were addressed to the administrators.
Plaintiff Saraffian brought her criticism to the other co-owners in letters
addressed to them. Eventually, she would direct her criticism – and her threats
– to all the co-owners.

[
18
]

We will examine in more details those threats
and insults but for the moment  suffice to say that they included saying that
the administrators were part of Organized Crime and that they were defrauding
the co-owners.

[
19
]

In 2003, after having been unable to collect
plaintiff’s condo fees, the Syndicate register a legal hypothec on her unit.
This prompted her to institute the present proceedings in damages for an amount
of 1 166 000 $. Few months before, she had instituted another proceeding in
damages for more than 900 000$ against the builder/promoter.

[
20
]

Plaintiff was not represented in any of the
proceedings. This, of course, made things more difficult. Furthermore,
procedurally, plaintiff contested everything under the sun making regular appearances
before the Court an ordinary fixture of the case.

[
21
]

For this reason, the special management of the
case was eventually ordered and given to Justice Israël Mass.

[
22
]

In 2007, defendants Reich and Pietrantonio
instituted their own action in damages for defamation against Mrs Saraffian.
Eventually, these cases were joined to plaintiff’s proceeding.

[
23
]

It took a lot of time for Mrs Saraffian’s case
to be ready for trial, more than 12 years in fact. In 2014, Chief Justice
Fournier put the three cases on the role and gave the parties 15 days of
hearing starting on October 31
st
, 2016.

[
24
]

Some weeks before trial, plaintiff was ordered
to produce her exhibits and a final list of her witnesses. She then indicated
to Justice Cohen that she would be seeking legal representation for the trial
and for this reason she would be seeking a postponement.

[
25
]

Neither occurred and trial started as scheduled.

[
26
]

Trial was difficult for plaintiff and by way of
consequence for all involved.

[
27
]

Plaintiff had come with over 200 exhibits that
were not separated nor identified by tabs, making the finding of an exhibit a
painstaking affair. Plaintiff was eventually asked to separate her exhibits by
tabs. But this did not settle another problem: many of the exhibits were not
uniformly identified. That meant for example that exhibit P-123 in plaintiff’s
stack was identified as P-121 in the stack remitted to the Court and yet bore
another number in the stack remitted to defendants’ attorney. To make matters
worse, an exhibit in one stack would be a document of three pages in one stack
but had only one page in another. To make matters even more unmanageable, when
Plaintiff wanted to refer to one of her exhibit, she often did not seem to
remember under which exhibit number it had been identified. This meant that
most of the time she had to go through her stack of exhibits to find the proper
one after minutes of exploration. Plaintiff regularly could not even say what
was the document she was looking for. At times, she would also say about
something that it was
documented
but she could not say by which one of
her exhibits. On many occasions, when she couldn’t find a document she was
thinking about in her exhibits, she would then say that she had it back home
and that she would bring it the following day or the following  week. Of
course, she never did.

[
28
]

On the first day of trial, plaintiff indicated
that she had difficulty finding her witnesses, it seems that she had not
contacted any of them yet. When the Court warned her of the importance of
producing her witnesses and that trial would proceed with or without them, she
finally produced three, two of which were totally irrelevant out of an original
list of 16 witnesses.

[
29
]

Plaintiff tried to tackle the problem by trying
to introduce into evidence letters or estimates from these absent witnesses. As
to be expected, this strategy soon ran into trouble when defendants’ attorney
objected. The Court sustained these objections explaining to plaintiff that she
could not have these witnesses testify indirectly by producing a document they
had written, because of defendants’ right to cross-examination.

[
30
]

Plaintiff had also to be reminded to stick to
the issues for which she was claiming. For example, she kept rehashing in her
testimony the issues she had had with the promoter/builder. She consequently
had trouble focusing on the relevant issues at hand.

[
31
]

A lot of time is lost because of plaintiff’s
unpreparedness.

[
32
]

It is against this factual backdrop that the
litigated issues must be examined.

ISSUES IN
DISPUTE

[
33
]

Plaintiff Saraffian alleges quite a number of
reproaches against the Syndicate but only a fraction translates into specific
claims.  They may be summarized as follows:

•

Has
plaintiff established occurrences for which the Syndicate is responsible?

o

The air infiltration
problem (2002/2003)

o

The burst pipe incident of
January 2004

o

The storage room incident
of 2008

•

In the
affirmative, has the Syndicate refused to make the required corrections or
repairs?

•

Has
plaintiff established the amount of damages directly cause by these
occurrences?

•

Have
the defendants Reich and Pietrantonio subjected plaintiff to “systematic
physical and mental suffering and harassment which resulted in mental torture”?

•

In the
affirmative, is plaintiff entitled to punitive damages for an amount 50 000$
from each of the two defendants?

[
34
]

Those are the issues contained in plaintiff’s
amended proceeding of December 3, 2008. At trial, plaintiff indicated that she
wanted to amend her proceeding in order to add other allegations pertaining to
a new set of conclusions. Plaintiff did not have the amendments in writing and
was asked to put them in writing. The written amendments were brought the
following week.

[
35
]

The amendments were objected to by the
defendants and the objection was sustained. Many other objections relating to
the filling of documents by plaintiff were also sustained.

[
36
]

Although none of these judgements on the
amendments and on the objections to the filling of documents were then
appealed, the Court finds it useful to give hereinafter a short summary of its
reasoning in this regard.

Amendments and
Objections to the filling of documents

Plaintiff’
S
amendments

[
37
]

On the first day of trial, plaintiff indicated
that she had amendments to bring to her proceeding. When asked if she had put
these amendments in writing, plaintiff responded by saying she didn’t have time
to do it. Plaintiff was asked then to put her amendments in writing. After
countless reminders by the court, the written amendment came on the
seventh

day of trial.

[
38
]

All these amendments except two that were
related to the questions already raised in the proceedings were dismissed
because they constituted new claims and might have implied a continuance. The
Court’s judgement on these amendments was not appealed.

Objections to plaintiff’s
written evidence

[
39
]

Most of plaintiff’s evidence consisted of
letters from third parties, newspaper clippings and documents establishing that
third parties had been convicted of criminal infractions.

[
40
]

A large number of the documents plaintiff wanted
to produce were newspapers clippings on a subject that had no relevancy with
the proceedings. As an example, an article dealt with the problems and
difficulties of co-ownership in Quebec. Plaintiff wanted to produce the cover
jacket of a book entitled: “
Without Conscience
:
The

disturbing
psychopaths among us”
.

[
41
]

A large number of these documents were letters addressed
to plaintiff or to third party. Plaintiff had been warned at the beginning of
the trial that she could not have the authors of these letters testify by
producing a letter from them, she had to bring them to trial. Even tough, she
had another week to do so, she did not. Other letters had the appearance of an
expert report. For obvious reasons these could not put in evidence without
their authors being called to the bar. Other documents were either invoices or
estimates for repairs. The objection to their filling was upheld because either
the repairs were not the object of a claim or the document was not clear as to
its object. The objection requiring the presence at trial of its authors was
consequently sustained.

[
42
]

It is important to note that the Court had early
on warned plaintiff that if she wanted to file these documents, she would have
to bring the appropriate witnesses. Plaintiff objected that she is not a lawyer
and that consequently she could not be expected to follow rules she had no
cognizance of.

[
43
]

Of course, the Court cannot apply the rules of
procedure and the rule of evidence to the party who has legal representation and
not to the party who has no legal representation. Furthermore, the Court doubts
the sincerity of plaintiff’s excuse in view of her extended procedural past.

[
44
]

Plaintiff tries to explain her evidence
misgivings by saying that it was not reasonable for the Court to expect that
she would have kept or obtained this kind of documentation. After all, she
says, this case dates back almost 14 years. The Court in her mind should
consequently relax the rules of evidence and consider that her word that what
she says was damaged and that the value of the items and the cost of the
repairs are what she says it is.

[
45
]

The Court did not accept plaintiff’s excuse that
she could not be expected to know these rules. First, there is only one set of
rules before our courts and that set of rules applies to everybody whether
represented or not. Second, the Court does not believe plaintiff when she says
she did not know. In his judgement in 2007 in another case involving plaintiff,
Justice Barbe had to deal with the same kind of excuse:

[9] L’appelante (Hanna Saraffian) déclare qu’elle se
représente elle-même et qu’elle s’y connaît en droit, puisqu’elle a fait des études
de droit aux États-Unis et qu’elle fût partie à une dizaine de procès au cours
des dernières années pour lesquels elle se représentait elle-même.

[…]

[23] Enfin, faut-il ajouter que si le TAQ avait
accepté en preuve la déclaration écrite d’un témoin absent, cela aurait eu pour
effet de priver l’autre partie de l’exercice d’un droit fondamental et péremptoire,
soit le droit au contre-interrogtoire, ce qui aurait constitué un accroc à la
justice naturelle […]
[2]
.

(the words between parentheses are added)

[
46
]

Third, when plaintiff was so informed, she had
still 13 days – including two weekends – to react. She did not. She had told
the Court from the outset that a lawyer she did not want to identify was
helping her. She had all the necessary time to adjust and call the appropriate
witnesses. She elected not to do so.

[
47
]

Consequently, almost all of plaintiff’s case rests
only on her impressions or suspicions. Unfortunately for her, in a court of
law, a ton of suspicion is not worth an ounce of evidence.

[
48
]

To make matters worse for plaintiff, the very
limited part of her claim that rests on her testimony and where she was able to
produce an estimation, defendants presented an opposing compelling defence.

[
49
]

In her argument, Mrs Saraffian submitted to the
Court judgments that were of no use, each of them being
un cas d’espèce

based on specific expert evidence about matters that had nothing to do with the
facts of our case.

[
50
]

The only substantive legal argument raised Mrs
Saraffian dealt with the objection on her producing of a letter from Dominique
Frenette. Mrs Sarrafian wanted to use this letter as an expert report. She
hadn’t produced it as such under art. 294.1 or 402 of the
Code of civil
procedure.
The objection was sustained and the letter was not introduced
into evidence during trial.

[
51
]

At the end of trial, during argument Mrs
Saraffian tried to relitigate the point even though it was too late to do so. Citing
art. 293 of the new
Code of Civil Procedure
, she argued that she was
entitled to:

Article 293 provides that:

293.
The report of an expert
stands in lieu of their testimony. To be admissible, the     expert report must
have been disclosed to the parties and filed in the record within the time
limits for disclosure and filing of evidence. Otherwise, it may be admitted
only if it was made available to the parties by another means in a timely
manner so that they could react and determine whether the expert’s presence
might be useful. It may however be admitted outside such time frames with leave
of the court.

[
52
]

For the sake of transparency, the Court
believes that even if art. 293 of the new Code applied to the matter at hand, it
would have to be read in conjunction with article 238 that states that:

238
. An expert report must be
brief but provide sufficient details to enable the court to make its own
assessment of the facts set out in the report and of the reasons that led to
the conclusions drawn by the expert. It must mention the analytical methodology
used.

[…]

[
53
]

It is clear that the letter does not meet these
requirements. Furthermore, the Court believes that the requisites of the new
Code

cannot apply to expert reports prepared under the previous
Code
. That is
why Mrs Sarrafian had to produce the letter under art. 294.1 or 402 C.p.c.

[
54
]

In any event, the letter is at best ambiguous
as what was the mandate and what it establishes. It appears much more as off
the cuff remarks than as a professional opinion.

[
55
]

Two other questions arise from the Syndicate’s
cross-claim:

•

Must plaintiff pay the
arrears of condo fees and has the Syndicate established the amount owed by
plaintiff in this regard?

•

Is the Syndicate entitled
to have its extrajudicial costs reimbursed by plaintiff for her abusive conduct
in the management of her case and in her use of the judicial process?

•

Is the Syndicate entitled
to punitive damages (50 000$)?

[
56
]

Each of the defendants Reich’s and Pietrantonio’s
proceeding bring the following questions:

•

Has Mrs
Saraffian made defamatory comments in their regard?

•

In the
affirmative, at what amount should the amount of moral damages be established?

•

Is Mrs
Saraffian responsible of any punitive damages and in the affirmative at what
amount should she be condemned in each case?

ANALYSIS

Preliminary remarks

[
57
]

In her proceeding, plaintiff makes eighteen
specific claims totalling an amount of almost 1.4 M $. At the start of the
trial when asked by the Court to concentrate on the facts that were relevant to
these claims, plaintiff indicated that she had no evidence to support eight of
those eighteen claims.

[
58
]

Within minutes of the start of the trial, the
Syndicate was then informed for the first time that it had no longer to face
eight claims totalling a sum of 795 700$. This will be subject of further
discussion when the Syndicate’s claim for the reimbursement of extrajudicial
costs will be examined.

[
59
]

Plaintiff removed the following claims:

•

18 000
$ for cost of the repainting of her unit

•

40 000
$ for the cost of maintaining a second house

•

180 000
$ for the loss of rental income from the second house

•

450 000
$ for the
indirect
loss of her home due to the
Evil actions of
defendants

•

60 000
$ for excessive mortgage rate

•

27 000
$ for water damage to storage room in 2002/2003

•

62 000
$ for her mother’s living expenses

•

2 700 $
for cost of rising insurance premium

[
60
]

Plaintiff proceeding was consequently reduced to
ten claims totalling an amount of 584 115 $. Out of those claims six are linked
directly to three events: the air infiltration problem of 2002/2003, the burst
pipe problem of 2004 and the water damage to the storage room incident of 2008.

Problems related to duct air infiltration
(2002/2003)

[
61
]

Plaintiff testified that two of her claims
relate to an alleged air circulation problem in her unit:

30 000 $ for the costs to correct
construction defects of the existing duct work located in    the common area of
her private fraction
[3]
;

75 000 $ for repairs and replacement of
damaged materials and contents […]
[4]

[
62
]

Plaintiff complains about the flow of air
circulation in her unit. She describes this problem in hyperbolic terms in her
proceedings and her letters of complaint:

[…] the draft enters her kitchen ducts from
the roof into her Range Hood
comes down
like a
CYCLON
[…]
[5]

(the Court underlines)

[
63
]

Although, this is not clear, she attributes some
damages to this backdraft problem. She seems to be claiming an amount of no
less than 75 000$ ”for the repairs and replacements of damaged materials and
contents in her private fraction”. She also claims a sum of 30 000 $ “for the
costs to correct construction defect of the existing duck work located in the
common area of her private fraction”.

[
64
]

The problem with Mrs SaraffIan’s claim starts
with her contradictory statements about when the problem would have started. In
her November 18
th
, 2002 letter (Exhibit P-57 (a) she says that the
problem existed when the promoter/builder controlled the Syndicate while in her
examination on discovery of November 17
th
, 2003, she says that it
only started under the new administration of the Syndicate.

[
65
]

She complained of the problem in her letter of
November 18
th
, 2002. The defendant Reich had just been elected few
days earlier. As we know, the Syndicate had plenty on their hands then. Yet,
they responded to plaintiff’s alleged problem early on.

[
66
]

A letter from the Syndicate dated December 10
th
,
2002 confirms numerous telephone conversations between defendant Reich and
plaintiff regarding the alleged problem and asking for plaintiff’s availability
for an inspection of her unit. Plaintiff had refused to give access to her unit
to a contractor hired by the Syndicate to address the problem.

[
67
]

More specifically, in his letter of December 10
th
,
2002 addressed to plaintiff by Ilan Reich of the Syndicate writes:

As promised during our last conversation on
Sunday, December 8
th
, we followed up on your said vent problems by
performing a complete maintenance on all building fans and make-up air units
and asked the ventilation company to visit your apartment to verify your unit’s
vent problems. I had phoned you on 2 occasions last night, around 7 : 15 pm and
left you a message that we would be knocking on your door to be given access.
We did so around 8pm, but unfortunately you declined to give us access to your
residence once you opened your door.

We understood from your last couple of
correspondences, that this issue was an emergency for you. This obviously does
not seem to be the case anymore.

In the event that you still feel that we
should get your vents looked into, please send your availabilities and we will
try to coordinate with the ventilation company.
[6]

[
68
]

Plaintiff never got back to the Syndicate in
this regard.

[
69
]

This particular letter was following one amongst
many long letters from plaintiff, which had quite another tone:

The purpose of this writing is to advise
you that our telephone conversation of yesterday was recorded.

[…] while you committed a CRIMINAL ACT by
dealing with me by EXTORSION […]
[7]

[
70
]

Considering this context where Mrs Saraffian was
complaining about almost everything and making all kinds of accusations and
threats, one can only appreciate Mr Reich and the Syndicate’s openness and
willingness to help.

[
71
]

Mr Reich had just been elected as an administrator
of the Syndicate and was scrambling with the other administrators (Mr Dario
Pietrantonio and Mr Claude Lambert) to get the affairs of the Syndicate under
control.

[
72
]

To make a long story short, the Syndicate was
never given access to Mrs Saraffian’s unit in order to investigate the problem
she was describing. Nevertheless, they had the ventilation equipment inspected
and everything was in order.

[
73
]

Meanwhile, plaintiff had the person who had
designed the air ventilation system (Mr Dominique Frenette) visit her unit in
January of 2003.  Plaintiff did not produce an expert report from Mr Frenette
so he was not allowed to give his opinion on the alleged air circulation
problem but was only permitted to testify as to the facts he noticed during his
visit. It is consequently only the description of what Mr Frenette noticed
during his visit that may be considered from his letter of January 24
th
,
2003 to plaintiff (Exhibit P-91).

[
74
]

In a nutshell, Mr Frenette totally contradicts
plaintiff’s contention and confirms that the excessive air circulation
entering

from the kitchen hood was impossible and that on the contrary air could only be

evacuated
from the kitchen. He had also noticed that the system had been
designed to bring air at 21 C when outside temperature is minus 28 C. During
his visit, the temperature in plaintiff’s unit was 17 C when outside
temperature was minus 20 C. He suggested that the thermostat of the duct system
be checked.

[
75
]

It was only after plaintiff instituted her
proceedings in the summer of 2003 that the problem resurfaced in her claim for
damages allegedly caused by it.

[
76
]

The Syndicate wanted to respond to these
complaints but they once again encountered plaintiff’s refusal to give them
access to her unit. The Syndicate had to obtain two court orders to be able to
have their experts enter plaintiff’s unit in order to evaluate the nature of
the problem she was complaining about. They also examined the air circulating
units on the roof of the property along with all the fans of the units.

[
77
]

The experts found nothing wrong. All the systems
were sound. The experts could find no back draft anywhere. In his testimony,
Mr. Ohanian explained why what plaintiff is saying cannot be: the systems are
designed to bring the air out. They cannot bring the air in. If defective the
systems would simply not take the air out, they would not bring air in.

[
78
]

Even the only witness called to testify by
plaintiff on that topic, Frenette, confirm that when he had gone on the
premises, he never noticed air
coming in
but only air
going out
.

[
79
]

This reality was also confirmed even in another
report that plaintiff tried unsuccessfully to produce in evidence. The
architect Cristian Andrei had noticed during his visit that plaintiff’s
“kitchen hood ‘Nutone” did not shut off by turning the control knob. The fan
ran continuously, creating air suction in the kitchen and therefore
uncomfortable air currents.” That problem was eventually repaired by plaintiff
because, as we will see hereinafter, the kitchen hood was working properly when
the Syndicate’s experts examined it.

[
80
]

The uncontested evidence further shows that all
the air circulation units were and still are inspected and maintained twice a
year.

[
81
]

As for the cold air plaintiff is complaining
about, the expert explained that the air brought in the corridors is treated to
a specified predetermined temperature whatever the outside temperature is. In
other words, that air is not the air taken directly from outside. Mr. Ohanian
adds that during his visit to plaintiff’s unit the outside temperature was 10
degrees and the thermostats inside her unit was set at 15 C.

[
82
]

Here again the Syndicate’s experts found nothing
wrong.

[
83
]

In their detailed report, they concluded:

The mechanical concepts, ventilation and
plumbing, used in this building are of common and standard practice. Our visit
and inspection apartment #306 (plaintiff’s unit) could not find any backdraft
problems originating from the roof to the apartment. This apartment being on
the 3
rd
floor and sharing common ventilation equipment and shafts
with other dwellings, located on the floors above and below, cannot have
isolated draft problems, other apartments would present the same discomforts.
The public corridors being pressurized, air would have a tendency of passing
through the apartment rather than being drawn down from the roof, especially
with back draft dampers being shown on the roof level at all mechanical shafts.

In general, the quality of the construction
and finishing can be considered standard, in good condition and corresponds to
the National Building Code specification. It also noticed that no other work
was done in the apartment since its purchase, to refresh the premises.
[8]

[
84
]

Mr Ohanian adds that the damages described by
plaintiff and shown on the pictures annexed to his report cannot have been
caused by any kind of back draft.

[
85
]

Finally, the uncontested evidence shows that
none of the other co-owners whose units are above or below Mrs Saraffian’s unit
complained about similar problems, even though they share the same ventilation
equipment and shafts as Mrs Saraffian. It would be physically impossible for
plaintiff to have this alleged problem without them having it too.

[
86
]

If plaintiff problem is related to cold
temperatures in her unit, many other explanations excluding the Syndicate’s
responsibility can be considered. During his visit to plaintiff unit in January
of 2003, Mr Frenette had given two telling examples of the culprits for this
situation. He had noticed that plaintiff own thermostats were set at 17 C while
the exterior temperature was minus 20 C. When the Syndicate’s expert visited
plaintiff premises her thermostats were at 15 C while the exterior temperature
was 10 C. It is obvious that plaintiff doesn’t mind cool temperatures in her
unit.  Mr Frenette had also indicated that his design of the ventilation system
was for an open space concept while plaintiff had asked to close up the kitchen
by adding a wall.

[
87
]

From this overwhelming evidence, the Court finds
that plaintiff has not discharged herself of the burden of establishing any
kind of air infiltration problems by her kitchen duct in her unit and that
those problems were the responsibility of the Syndicate.

[
88
]

Considering the expenditures of time, money and

As we all know since the case of

, it
is only in exceptional cases where there is an abuse of the right to institute
legal proceedings that a party may claim reimbursement of its legal costs.
Justice Rochon reminded us that there is fundamental difference between an
abuse on the merits of a case (
abus sur le fond
) and an abuse on the
right to institute legal proceedings:

74. Avant d'examiner plus avant cette question, il
importe de distinguer et de définir l'abus de droit sur le fond du litige
(l'abus sur le fond) de l'abus du droit d'ester en justice.
L'abus sur le fond intervient avant que ne
débutent les procédures judiciaires. L'abus sur le fond se produit au moment de
la faute contractuelle ou extracontractuelle. Il a pour effet de qualifier
cette faute. La partie abuse de son droit par une conduite répréhensible,
outrageante, abusive, de mauvaise foi. Au moment où l'abus sur le fond se cristallise,
il n'y a aucune procédure judiciaire d'entreprise. C'est précisément cet abus
sur le fond qui incitera la partie adverse à s'adresser aux tribunaux pour
obtenir la sanction d'un droit ou une juste réparation.

75. À l'opposé, l'abus du droit d'ester en
justice est une faute commise à l'occasion d'un recours judiciaire. C'est le
cas où la contestation judiciaire est, au départ, de mauvaise foi, soit en
demande ou en défense. Ce sera encore le cas lorsqu'une partie de mauvaise foi,
multiplie les procédures, poursuit inutilement et abusivement un débat
judiciaire.

76. Je formule la question qui nous est
posée comme suit : la conduite répréhensible, abusive et de mauvaise foi d'une
partie sur le fond du litige permet-elle en soi à la partie adverse de réclamer
les honoraires extrajudiciaires de son avocat à titre de dommages-intérêts ?

77. Soit dit avec égards, les principes de
la responsabilité civile m'incitent à apporter une réponse négative à la
question posée. En principe et sauf circonstances exceptionnelles, les
honoraires payés par une partie à son avocat ne peuvent, à mon avis, être
considérés comme un dommage direct qui sanctionne un abus sur le fond. Il
n'existe pas de lien de causalité adéquat entre la faute (abus sur le fond) et
le dommage. La causalité adéquate correspond à ou aux événements ayant un
rapport logique, direct et immédiat avec l'origine du préjudice subi. Seul
l'abus du droit d'ester en justice peut être sanctionné par l'octroi de tels
dommages. Il m'apparaît erroné de transformer l'abus sur le fond en un abus du
droit d'ester en justice dès qu'un recours judiciaire est entrepris. Quelques
explications s'imposent.

78. Il est acquis au débat qu'une partie ne
peut, règle générale, être compensée des honoraires payés à son avocat pour
faire valoir ses droits. Le justiciable devra payer ces honoraires
extrajudiciaires qu'il y ait ou non abus sur le fond. Les honoraires ne
seraient d'ailleurs pas encourus si la partie adverse reconnaissait, dès le
début des procédures judiciaires, sa faute même si cette dernière peut être
qualifiée d'abus sur le fond (conduite abusive, répréhensible, scandaleuse,
outrageante, de mauvaise foi). Dans ce cas, malgré la conduite abusive sur le
fond, la partie n'aurait pas à débourser inutilement des honoraires à son
avocat. Cet exemple démontre l'absence de lien de causalité suffisant entre la
faute et le dommage.

79. À l'inverse, peu importe qu'il y ait
abus ou non sur le fond, une partie qui abuse de son droit d'ester en justice
causera un dommage à la partie adverse qui, pour combattre cet abus paie
inutilement des honoraires judiciaires à son avocat. Il y a, dans ce cas, un
véritable lien de causalité entre la faute et le dommage.

[
160
]

From the foregoing, the
Court cannot award a claim for the judicial costs of a party to a proceeding
even though that proceeding is dismissed for having no foundation in law and
even if that absence of foundation was obvious to the point of being scandalous
(
abus sur le fond
).

Relevant factors in the determination of the punitive damages

[
211
]

The court is well aware that when a claim for
punitive damages is made, it must decide with caution, bearing. in mind the
teachings of our Supreme Court on what an adequate award should be:

[188] This appeal highlights the
problems trial judges face in calculating punitive damages.  Although they
have a discretion in this regard, they must exercise it judicially and must
also, to the extent possible, comply with the practice established by the
courts and consider all the specific circumstances of each case, bearing in
mind the principles of deterrence, punishment and denunciation that underlie
punitive damages.

[190] It should be borne in mind that a
trial court has latitude in determining the quantum of punitive damages,
provided that the amount it awards remains within rational limits in light of
the specific circumstances of the case before it.

[
212
]

The Supreme Court reminds us that “the gravity
of the fault is undoubtedly the most important factor”
[37]
.

[200] The gravity of the fault is
undoubtedly the most important factor (Genex Communications inc. v. Association
québécoise de l’industrie du disque, du spectacle et de la vidéo,
2009 QCCA
2201
,
[2009] R.J.Q. 2743
; Fondation québécoise du cancer v. Patenaude,
2006
QCCA 1554
,
[2007] R.R.A. 5
; Voltec ltée v. CJMF FM ltée,
2002 CanLII 63224 (QC CA)
,
[2002] R.R.A. 1078
(C.A.)
; Baudouin, Jobin and Vézina, at para.
912).  It is assessed from two perspectives:  the wrongful conduct of
the wrongdoer and the seriousness of the infringement of the victim’s rights.
According to Claude Dallaire, the courts consider the gravity of the conduct
and its impact on the victim (pp. 127 et seq.).  The analysis of the evidence
will therefore be focused sometimes on the offender’s conduct and sometimes on
the effect of that conduct on the victim (Procureur général du Québec v.
Boisclair,
2001 CanLII 20655 (QC CA)
,
[2001] R.J.Q. 2449 (C.A.)
, at paras.
9
‑
10
).
In either case, it must be borne in mind that a myriad of contextual factors
can be taken into account in the analysis.  If, for example, the evidence shows
that the contract was abusive, that the merchant committed a fault and gained
an undue competitive advantage by doing so, or that the consumers who were
victims of the practice were particularly vulnerable, these facts will
obviously be relevant to the assessment of the gravity of the fault.

[202]  The third factor mentioned in art.
1621, para. 2 C.C.Q., the extent of the reparation already awarded under other
heads, is an analytical criterion that has been used frequently (St
‑
Ferdinand; Augustus v. Gosset,
1996 CanLII 173 (SCC)
,
[1996] 3
S.C.R. 268
; Lambert v. Macara,
2004 CanLII 30445 (QC CA)
,
[2004] R.J.Q. 2637 (C.A.)
).  According to it,
the court must not award punitive damages unless compensatory damages are not
enough to discourage repetition either because their amount is too small or
because they will have no impact on the debtor’s financial situation.  However,
this principle does not change the independent nature of punitive damages.
Even if an award of compensatory damages is generous, it will not necessarily
preclude an award of punitive damages.

[
213
]

Here, the Court believes that a condamnation to

dismal effect on plaintiff. Plaintiff doesn’t fear the judicial system. On the

[203] Finally, the purpose of the fourth
factor mentioned in
art. 1621
, para. 2 C.C.Q. is to adjust the quantum of
punitive damages on the basis of the total amount the debtor will have to pay
personally.  This assessment ensures that the amount of the award will actually
have the intended effect on the offender.  The amount may sometimes have to be
varied where a third person is paying, since the objective of preventing
repetition is then achieved through an intermediary.  The person actually
paying must thus be punished to motivate that person to encourage the wrongdoer
to change his or her ways.  Closely related to this consideration, another
purpose of this factor is to evaluate the real utility of the second of the
factors mentioned in
art. 1621
, para. 2 C.C.Q., namely the debtor’s patrimonial
situation.  Thus, where the debtor of the obligation will not personally be
paying the amount of the award of punitive damages, there is no need to assess
his or her patrimony to determine that amount.
[38]

(b)   Other Criteria to be considered:

criminal history of the person guilty of a violation may be a relevant factor.

whose previous conduct has been exemplary may therefore differ from the amount
awarded against one who has been involved in many serious prior offences
(Whiten, at para. 69; Dallaire, at pp. 136
‑
42 and 164
‑
65).

Based on these expenses, the court finds that
plaintiff’s real revenues are of at least 50 000$ a year.

[
234
]

For these reasons, the Court concludes that
plaintiff’s patrimonial situation does not constitute an obstacle to an award
for punitive damages.

The amount for punitive damages

[
235
]

Establishing the amount of punitive damages that
should be awarded is always a subjective task. Although as a general rule the
amount must remain reasonable, the actual amount is a matter of judicial
discretion.

[
236
]

The jurisprudence highlights many relevant
conditions that may be considered in order to arrive at an adequate amount.
Among those conditions, the Court may take into account among other things the
background and the conduct of the abusive party, the notoriety of the victim,
the extent of the compensatory damages awarded, the nature of the abuse.
[40]

[
237
]

As we have seen, the Syndicate is asking for an
award of 50 000$ for punitive damages.

[
238
]

As we will see hereinafter, the defendants
Pietrantonio and Reich are also asking amounts of 50 000$ and 25 000$
respectively in this regard. As we will see, a recurrence of this kind of
conduct is more likely against the Syndicate than against them. As we know,
both have left the condominium since almost 10 years and they don’t have any
relationship with her anymore.

[
239
]

In this context, the award for punitive damages
should be higher for the Syndicate than for the defendants Pietrantonio and Reich.

[
240
]

The Court must also take into consideration the
fact that it has condemned plaintiff to reimburse some of the defendants’ legal
cost.

[
241
]

The Court finds that an amount of 25 000$ for
the Syndicate is in order in the circumstances.
